docs.text:
utility-viz 2.0 is in beta

utility-viz 2.0.0b1 is a pre-release. The stable line stays econ-viz 1.x until 2.0 final is released. Pre-releases are skipped by default, so the commands below pass --prerelease allow. Coming from econ-viz? See Migration guide.

With uv, create a project and add it as a dependency:

uv init my-diagrams
cd my-diagrams
uv add --prerelease allow utility-viz

Run scripts inside the project environment with uv run:

uv run python main.py

docs.title: Optional dependencies
docs.text:
Extras enable features that require additional packages:

uv add --prerelease allow "utility-viz[animation]"    # GIF export (Pillow)
uv add --prerelease allow "utility-viz[interactive]"  # notebook widgets
uv add --prerelease allow "utility-viz[all]"          # all extras

docs.title: Global CLI installation
docs.text:
To use only the command-line interface, install it as a standalone tool so utility-viz is available on your PATH:

uv tool install --prerelease allow utility-viz

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/EconViz/utility-viz.git
cd utility-viz
uv sync --all-extras

uv sync installs the dev dependency group by default; --all-extras also installs every optional dependency. Run the test suite with:

uv run pytest

docs.title: Verifying the installation
docs.text:
uv run utility-viz --version
uv run utility-viz help

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
from utility_viz import Canvas, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas

model = CobbDouglas(alpha=0.5, beta=0.5)
eq = solve(model, px=2.0, py=3.0, income=30.0)
lvls = levels.around(eq.utility, n=5)

cvs = Canvas(
    x_max=20,
    y_max=15,
    x_label="x",
    y_label="y",
    title=r"Cobb-Douglas $x^{0.5} y^{0.5}$",
)
cvs.add_utility(model, levels=lvls)
cvs.add_budget(2.0, 3.0, 30.0, fill=True)
cvs.add_equilibrium(eq, show_ray=True)
cvs.save("cobb_douglas.png")

docs.title: Choose a model
docs.text:
Pick a utility function from utility_viz.models. See the Model catalogue for the full list.

from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas

model = CobbDouglas(alpha=0.5, beta=0.5)

docs.title: Solve for the equilibrium
docs.text:
solve() returns an Equilibrium named tuple with fields x, y, utility, and bundle_type.

from utility_viz import solve

eq = solve(model, px=2.0, py=3.0, income=30.0)
print(eq.x, eq.y, round(eq.utility, 3))

# 7.5 5.0 6.124

docs.title: Utility levels
docs.text:
from utility_viz import levels

# 5 curves around the optimum
lvls = levels.around(eq.utility, n=5)

docs.title: Build the canvas
docs.text:
from utility_viz import Canvas

cvs = Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15)

docs.title: Add layers
docs.text:
Canvas methods return self, so calls can be chained:

cvs.add_utility(model, levels=lvls)
cvs.add_budget(2.0, 3.0, 30.0, fill=True)
cvs.add_equilibrium(eq, show_ray=True)

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
Raster / vectorInteractive 
# PNG
cvs.save("figure.png")
# PDF
cvs.save("figure.pdf")
# SVG
cvs.save("figure.svg")

# interactive window
cvs.show()

docs.title: Using the LaTeX parser
docs.text:
from utility_viz import parse_latex, Canvas, levels, solve

model = parse_latex(r"x^{0.4} y^{0.6}")
eq = solve(model, px=2.0, py=3.0, income=30.0)
lvls = levels.around(eq.utility, n=5)

Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15).add_utility(
    model, levels=lvls
).add_budget(2.0, 3.0, 30.0).add_equilibrium(eq).save(
    "figure.png"
)

docs.title: Multi-panel figures
docs.text:
Figure lets you compose several Canvas panels into one layout.

from utility_viz import Figure, Layout, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas

fig = Figure(
    Layout.SIDE_BY_SIDE,
    x_max=20,
    y_max=15,
    x_label="x",
    y_label="y",
    title="Before / After Price Change",
    shared_y=True,
)

cases = [
    (
        CobbDouglas(alpha=0.5, beta=0.5),
        2.0,
        3.0,
        30.0,
        r"Before: $p_x=2$",
    ),
    (
        CobbDouglas(alpha=0.3, beta=0.7),
        4.0,
        3.0,
        30.0,
        r"After: $p_x=4$",
    ),
]

for idx, (model, px, py, income, title) in enumerate(cases):
    eq = solve(model, px=px, py=py, income=income)
    panel = fig[idx]
    panel.ax.set_title(title)
    panel.add_utility(
        model, levels=levels.around(eq.utility, n=5)
    )
    panel.add_budget(px, py, income, fill=True)
    panel.add_equilibrium(eq, show_ray=True)

fig.save("comparison.png")

docs.title: Demand diagrams
docs.text:
Use PricePath plus DemandDiagram to link the goods-space optimum to Marshallian demand.

from utility_viz import DemandDiagram, LinearBudget, PricePath
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas

model = CobbDouglas(alpha=0.5, beta=0.5)
budget = LinearBudget(px=2.0, py=2.0, income=40.0)
path = PricePath(
    model,
    budget=budget,
    price="px",
    price_range=(0.8, 6.0),
    n=40,
)

fig = DemandDiagram(path, title="Demand: Cobb-Douglas")
fig.add_marshallian_panel(price_markers=[1.5, 4.0])
fig.save("demand.png")

docs.title: Animation
docs.text: utility-viz includes a lightweight GIF workflow built around Animator. The API stays close to normal plotting: you write a frame factory that returns a fresh Canvas or Figure, then sweep a numeric frame sequence and save the result as a GIF.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
uv add "utility-viz[animation]"

If you also want notebook widgets, install:

uv add "utility-viz[all]"

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from utility_viz import Canvas, levels, solve
from utility_viz.animation import Animator
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas


def draw(px: float) -> Canvas:
    model = CobbDouglas(alpha=0.5, beta=0.5)
    eq = solve(model, px=px, py=2.0, income=20.0)
    lvls = levels.around(eq.utility, n=5)

    return (
        Canvas(
            x_max=14,
            y_max=12,
            x_label="X_1",
            y_label="X_2",
            title="Price sweep",
        )
        .add_utility(model, levels=lvls)
        .add_budget(px=px, py=2.0, income=20.0, fill=True)
        .add_equilibrium(eq, show_ray=True, drop_dashes=True)
    )


Animator(draw, frames=np.linspace(1.0, 6.0, 45)).save(
    "price_sweep.gif",
    fps=12,
    dpi=120,
)

docs.title: Teaching sweeps
docs.text:
The local example script at examples/animation.py now generates three separate sweep families:

  • Parameter sweeps: move one utility-function parameter while holding prices and income fixed.
  • Price sweeps: hold the utility function fixed and sweep \(p_x\) while holding \(p_y\) fixed.
  • Income sweeps: hold the utility function and prices fixed and move only income.
  • Budget-only sweeps: remove the utility layer entirely so students can isolate budget-line motion.

The docs site embeds the same GIF assets directly, so what you see here matches the locally generated examples.

docs.title: Parameter sweeps
docs.text:
Vary utility-function parameters to see how the shape of the preference map changes.

Cobb-Douglas Vary \(\alpha\) while \(\beta = 1 - \alpha\) CES Vary \(\rho\) to change curvature and substitutability Perfect substitutes Vary \(a\) with \(b\) fixed Leontief Vary \(a\) with \(b\) fixed to move the kink path

docs.title: Price sweeps
docs.text:
Hold the utility function and background indifference-curve levels fixed, then vary one good's price to trace equilibrium as the budget line rotates.

Cobb-Douglas Price sweep with \(p_y\) fixed CES Price sweep with a fixed utility surface Perfect substitutes Under a rotating budget line Leontief Price sweep with fixed right-angle indifference curves Budget only Price sweep for isolating pure rotation of the constraint

docs.title: Income sweeps
docs.text:
Hold the utility function and prices fixed, then vary income to trace equilibrium as the budget line shifts in parallel.

Cobb-Douglas Income sweep with fixed prices CES Income sweep with fixed prices and fixed utility function Perfect substitutes Income sweep Leontief Income sweep with fixed prices Budget only Income sweep for isolating parallel shifts in the constraint

docs.title: Export notes
docs.text:
GIF export follows these rules:

  • Animator.save() uses Pillow, so no ffmpeg dependency is required.
  • GIF frames are composited onto white before export to prevent frame stacking artifacts.
  • fps, dpi, and loop are configurable per animation.

docs.title: Canvas
docs.text: Canvas is the central drawing surface. It manages a single matplotlib figure styled in the convention of microeconomic textbook diagrams: first-quadrant axes, arrow tips, LaTeX-rendered labels, and no numeric tick marks.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
Canvas(
    x_max: float,
    y_max: float,
    x_label: str,
    y_label: str,
    title: str | Label | None,
    dpi: int,
    x_label_pos: LabelPosition | str,
    y_label_pos: LabelPosition | str,
    theme: Theme | None,
    font: str | Sequence[str] | None,
    math_font: str | None,
    axis_stroke: Stroke | None,
    x_axis_stroke: Stroke | None,
    y_axis_stroke: Stroke | None,
    x_axis: Axis | None,
    y_axis: Axis | None,
) → Canvas
x_maxfloatDefault: 10.0

Upper bound of the horizontal axis

y_maxfloatDefault: 10.0

Upper bound of the vertical axis

x_labelstrDefault: 'X'

Shorthand for Axis(label=...) on the horizontal axis

y_labelstrDefault: 'Y'

Shorthand for Axis(label=...) on the vertical axis

titlestr or Label or NoneDefault: None

Figure title

dpiintDefault: 300

Raster export resolution (clamped to 1–1200)

x_label_posLabelPosition or strDefault: LabelPosition.RIGHT

Shorthand for Axis(label_position=...): above, right of, or below the arrow tip

y_label_posLabelPosition or strDefault: LabelPosition.TOP

Shorthand for Axis(label_position=...): left of, above, or right of the arrow tip

themeTheme or NoneDefault: None

Colour and style theme

fontstr or Sequence[str] or NoneDefault: None

Font family or fallback list for every text element

math_fontstr or NoneDefault: None

Matplotlib math font: dejavusans, dejavuserif, cm, stix, or stixsans

axis_strokeStroke or NoneDefault: None

Shared width, style, colour, and arrowhead for both axes

x_axis_strokeStroke or NoneDefault: None

Horizontal-axis override, shorthand for Axis(stroke=...)

y_axis_strokeStroke or NoneDefault: None

Vertical-axis override, shorthand for Axis(stroke=...)

x_axisAxis or NoneDefault: None

Label, label position, and stroke of the horizontal axis

y_axisAxis or NoneDefault: None

Label, label position, and stroke of the vertical axis

View example 
from utility_viz import ArrowStyle, Axis, Canvas, Stroke, themes

cvs = Canvas(
    x_max=20,
    y_max=15,
    title=r"Cobb-Douglas $x^{0.5} y^{0.5}$",
    dpi=300,
    font="DejaVu Sans",
    math_font="stix",
    axis_stroke=Stroke(width=1.0, arrow=ArrowStyle.TRIANGLE),
    # "top", "right", or "bottom"
    x_axis=Axis(label="x", label_position="right"),
    # "left", "top", or "right"
    y_axis=Axis(label="y", label_position="top"),
    theme=themes.default,
)

When the same setting is given twice, the Axis field wins. For the axis line, the order from highest to lowest is Axis.stroke, x_axis_stroke, axis_stroke, x_line_style / x_arrow_style, and theme.axis_stroke.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: All drawing methods return self, so calls can be chained.

docs.title: Utility curves
docs.text:
Draws indifference curves for a utility model. Pass an integer to levels for automatically spaced curves, or a list of utility values, such as levels.around(eq.utility, n=5), to place them around the optimum.

Canvas.add_utility(
    func: Callable,
    levels: int | list,
    color: str | None,
    linewidth: float | None,
    show_rays: bool,
    show_kinks: bool,
    kink_radius: float,
    show_bliss: bool,
    label: str | None,
    show_ic_labels: bool,
    ic_label_fmt: str,
    stroke: Stroke | None,
    ray_stroke: Stroke | None,
    kink_marker: Marker | None,
    bliss_marker: Marker | None,
    ic_label: Label | None,
    bliss_label: str | Label | None,
    highlight_level: float | None,
    secondary_stroke: Stroke | None,
    label_style: str,
    **kwargs,
) → Canvas
funcCallableRequired

Utility model to draw.

levelsint or listDefault: 3

Number of curves, or an explicit list of utility levels.

colorstr or NoneDefault: None

Colour override; otherwise uses the theme.

linewidthfloat or NoneDefault: None

Line width override; otherwise uses the theme.

show_raysboolDefault: False

Draw kink-locus rays for kinked utility models.

show_kinksboolDefault: False

Mark kink points on each indifference curve.

kink_radiusfloatDefault: 1.0

Size factor for kink markers.

show_blissboolDefault: True

Mark the bliss point when the model provides one.

labelstr or NoneDefault: None

Optional label in LaTeX math notation.

show_ic_labelsboolDefault: False

Show utility labels at curve ends.

ic_label_fmtstrDefault: '{:.2g}'

Format string for numeric utility labels.

strokeStroke or NoneDefault: None

Line style; overrides individual colour, width, and style shortcuts.

ray_strokeStroke or NoneDefault: None

Style of the rays; otherwise uses the theme.

kink_markerMarker or NoneDefault: None

Style of kink markers; otherwise uses the theme.

bliss_markerMarker or NoneDefault: None

Style of the bliss-point marker; otherwise uses the theme.

ic_labelLabel or NoneDefault: None

Style of labels at indifference-curve ends.

bliss_labelstr or Label or NoneDefault: None

Text or Label object for the bliss point.

highlight_levelfloat or NoneDefault: None

Emphasize the curve nearest this utility level.

secondary_strokeStroke or NoneDefault: None

Style of curves other than the highlighted curve.

label_stylestrDefault: 'numeric'

Use numeric values or ordinal textbook labels.

**kwargsKeyword arguments

Additional options forwarded to the underlying renderer or exporter.

docs.title: Focal and secondary curves
docs.text:
Pass the equilibrium utility to highlight_level to emphasize the nearest available level without drawing a second contour set yourself. The other levels use theme.secondary_ic_stroke, or an explicit secondary_stroke.

from utility_viz import Canvas, Stroke, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas

model = CobbDouglas(0.5, 0.5)
eq = solve(model, px=2, py=3, income=30)
lvls = levels.around(eq.utility, n=5)

(
    Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15)
    .add_utility(
        model,
        levels=lvls,
        highlight_level=eq.utility,
        secondary_stroke=Stroke(width=1, opacity=0.35),
        show_ic_labels=True,
        label_style="ordinal",
    )
    .add_budget(2, 3, 30, fill=True)
    .add_equilibrium(eq)
)

label_style="numeric" uses the formatted utility values; "ordinal" produces textbook labels \(u_1,u_2,\ldots\). Labels follow the local curve angle and are kept away from the visible boundary.

  • Before — every level has the same visual weight.
  • After — the equilibrium level is focal.
  • Ordinal labels — curves are labelled \(u_1,u_2,\ldots\).

docs.title: Budget line
docs.text:
Draws the budget line \(p_x x + p_y y = I\). Set fill=True to shade the feasible set below it.

Canvas.add_budget(
    px: float,
    py: float,
    income: float,
    color: str | None,
    linewidth: float | None,
    linestyle: str | None,
    label: str | None,
    fill: bool | Fill,
    fill_alpha: float | None,
    stroke: Stroke | None,
) → Canvas
pxfloatRequired

Price of good X; must be positive.

pyfloatRequired

Price of good Y; must be positive.

incomefloatRequired

Total budget; must be positive.

colorstr or NoneDefault: None

Colour override; otherwise uses the theme.

linewidthfloat or NoneDefault: None

Line width override; otherwise uses the theme.

linestylestr or NoneDefault: None

Matplotlib line style; otherwise uses the theme.

labelstr or NoneDefault: None

Optional label in LaTeX math notation.

fillbool or FillDefault: False

Shade the feasible set with True, or supply a Fill for colour and opacity.

fill_alphafloat or NoneDefault: None

Shading opacity; a supplied Fill opacity takes precedence.

strokeStroke or NoneDefault: None

Line style; overrides individual colour, width, and style shortcuts.

docs.title: Equilibrium
docs.text:
Marks the optimal bundle and drops dashed lines to both axes. Pass the result of solve() as eq; show_ray=True also draws the expansion path through the origin.

Canvas.add_equilibrium(
    eq: Equilibrium,
    color: str | None,
    markersize: float | None,
    label: str | Label | None,
    drop_dashes: bool,
    show_ray: bool,
    drop_stroke: Stroke | None,
    ray_stroke: Stroke | None,
    marker: Marker | None,
) → Canvas
eqEquilibriumRequired

Equilibrium returned by solve().

colorstr or NoneDefault: None

Colour override; otherwise uses the theme.

markersizefloat or NoneDefault: None

Marker size; otherwise uses the theme.

labelstr or Label or NoneDefault: 'x^*'

Optional label in LaTeX math notation.

drop_dashesboolDefault: True

Draw perpendicular guides to both axes.

show_rayboolDefault: False

Draw the ray from the origin through the equilibrium.

drop_strokeStroke or NoneDefault: None

Style of the guides to both axes.

ray_strokeStroke or NoneDefault: None

Style of the rays; otherwise uses the theme.

markerMarker or NoneDefault: None

Marker colour, size, and shape; otherwise uses the theme.

docs.title: Ray
docs.text:
Draws a dashed ray from the origin with slope slope (\(\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}x\)), often used for an expansion path or a fixed consumption ratio.

Canvas.add_ray(
    slope: float,
    color: str | None,
    linewidth: float | None,
    stroke: Stroke | None,
) → Canvas
slopefloatRequired

Ray slope, expressed as \(\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}x\).

colorstr or NoneDefault: None

Colour override; otherwise uses the theme.

linewidthfloat or NoneDefault: None

Line width override; otherwise uses the theme.

strokeStroke or NoneDefault: None

Line style; overrides individual colour, width, and style shortcuts.

docs.title: Point
docs.text:
Marks any point, such as a bundle to compare with the optimum. label is rendered in LaTeX math mode; pass a Label to move or restyle it.

Canvas.add_point(
    x: float,
    y: float,
    label: str | Label | None,
    color: str | None,
    markersize: float | None,
    offset: tuple[float, float] | None,
    marker: Marker | None,
) → Canvas
xfloatRequired

Horizontal coordinate of the point.

yfloatRequired

Vertical coordinate of the point.

labelstr or Label or NoneDefault: None

Optional label in LaTeX math notation.

colorstr or NoneDefault: None

Colour override; otherwise uses the theme.

markersizefloat or NoneDefault: None

Marker size; otherwise uses the theme.

offsettuple[float, float] or NoneDefault: None

Label offset (dx, dy) in points. A Label position or offset takes precedence.

markerMarker or NoneDefault: None

Marker colour, size, and shape; otherwise uses the theme.

docs.title: Show and save
docs.text:
show() opens an interactive window. save() infers the format from the file extension: .png, .pdf, .svg, or .tex for TikZ. It also releases matplotlib resources, so call it last.

Canvas.show() → None
Canvas.save(
    path: str,
    **kwargs,
) → None
pathstrRequired

Destination path; its extension selects PNG, PDF, SVG, or TikZ output.

**kwargsKeyword arguments

Additional options forwarded to the underlying renderer or exporter.

# interactive window
cvs.show()
# .png / .pdf / .svg / .tex
cvs.save("figure.png")

docs.title: Styles
docs.text:
Each kind of element has its own style object. Fields left as None keep the theme default, so set only what you want to change.

Stroke

Line width, line style, colour, arrowhead

Theme defaults — theme.budget_stroke, theme.ic_stroke, …

Marker

Point colour, size, shape

Theme defaults — theme.eq_marker, theme.point_marker, …

Label

Text, position, offset, colour, size, visibility

Theme defaults — theme.point_label, theme.axis_label, …

Legend

Legend position, size, frame, columns

Theme defaults — theme.legend

Fill

Shading colour and opacity

Theme defaults — theme.budget_fill

Axis

One axis's label, label position, and stroke

Theme defaults — none

Every object also takes an opacity from 0 (transparent) to 1 (opaque).

from utility_viz import Canvas, Fill, Label, Marker, Stroke

(
    Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15)
    .add_utility(
        model,
        levels=lvls,
        ic_label=Label(text="U={:.1f}", position="top"),
    )
    .add_budget(
        2.0,
        3.0,
        30.0,
        stroke=Stroke(color="black"),
        fill=Fill(color="lightgrey", opacity=0.4),
    )
    .add_equilibrium(
        eq,
        marker=Marker(color="#C0392B", shape="s"),
        label=Label(position="bottom-left", offset=8),
    )
    .add_point(
        12.0, 2.0, label=Label(text="A", position="left")
    )
    .save("styles.png")
)

Stroke is the preferred way to style lines. The separate color, linewidth, and linestyle arguments still work as shorthand and draw the same thing. A label takes its point's Marker colour unless it sets its own; label positions are top, bottom, left, right, and the four corners such as top-right, and Label(visible=False) hides a label.

docs.title: Text and legend
docs.text:
Every piece of text takes a Label: axis labels through Axis(label=...), the origin through origin_label, and the title through title. Legends go where they cover the least of the diagram, moving outside the plot area when every corner is taken; a Legend chooses an inside corner ("upper left", …) or a side outside ("top", "bottom", "left", "right").

from utility_viz import Axis, Canvas, Label, Legend

cvs = Canvas(
    title=Label(text="Cobb-Douglas", fontsize=13),
    x_axis=Axis(label=Label(text="x_1", fontsize=16)),
    origin_label=Label(visible=False),
)
cvs.show_legend(legend=Legend(position="bottom", fontsize=10))

The line and arrow styles below apply to the axes with the x_* and y_* parameters, and to any other line through Stroke.

docs.title: Line styles
docs.text:
Use LineStyle.SOLID, DASHED, DOTTED, or DASHDOT for axis lines. The equivalent strings—solid, dashed, dotted, and dashdot—are also accepted. Use Stroke(style=...) to apply the same setting to any other line.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from utility_viz import Canvas, LineStyle

styles = [
    LineStyle.SOLID,
    LineStyle.DASHED,
    LineStyle.DOTTED,
    LineStyle.DASHDOT,
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(7, 7))
for ax, style in zip(axes.flat, styles):
    Canvas(
        title=style.value,
        x_line_style=style,
        y_line_style=style,
        fig=fig,
        ax=ax,
    )

fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("line_styles.png", dpi=160, transparent=True)

docs.title: Arrow styles
docs.text:
Use ArrowStyle.SIMPLE, TRIANGLE, FANCY, or WEDGE for axis arrowheads. Use Stroke(arrow=...) to add the same arrowhead to another visible line.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from utility_viz import ArrowStyle, Canvas

styles = [
    ArrowStyle.SIMPLE,
    ArrowStyle.TRIANGLE,
    ArrowStyle.FANCY,
    ArrowStyle.WEDGE,
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(7, 7))
for ax, style in zip(axes.flat, styles):
    Canvas(
        title=style.name.title(),
        x_arrow_style=style,
        y_arrow_style=style,
        fig=fig,
        ax=ax,
    )

fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("arrow_styles.png", dpi=160, transparent=True)

Stroke is also available for paths, decomposition diagrams, DemandDiagram, Figure, and EdgeworthBox. Fields left as None inherit from the active theme.

docs.title: Method chaining
docs.text:
Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15).add_utility(
    model, levels=lvls
).add_budget(2.0, 3.0, 30.0, fill=True).add_equilibrium(
    eq, show_ray=True
).save(
    "figure.png"
)

docs.title: Settings File
docs.text: Keep your colours, lines, labels, and legend settings in an utility-viz.toml file and load them once, instead of passing the same arguments to every method.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
Section names match Theme properties, and fields match the arguments of the style objects. Anything left out keeps the built-in default.

# utility-viz.toml
base = "default"                 # default or nord

[font]
text = "TeX Gyre Pagella"
math = "stix"

[color]
ic = "#2E86AB"
budget = "#6C3483"
equilibrium = "#C0392B"

[stroke.budget]                  # theme.budget_stroke
width = 1.5
style = "solid"

[stroke.ic]                      # theme.ic_stroke
width = 1.8
opacity = 0.9

[marker.equilibrium]             # theme.eq_marker
size = 5

[label.point]                    # theme.point_label
fontsize = 12
position = "top-right"

[label.origin]
visible = false

[fill.budget]                    # theme.budget_fill
color = "lightgrey"
opacity = 0.3

[legend]                         # theme.legend
position = "auto"
fontsize = 10
base

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
from utility_viz import Canvas, Config

# diagrams created from now on
Config.load("utility-viz.toml").use()
# uses the file's settings
Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15)

theme = Config.load("utility-viz.toml").theme
# or one diagram only
Canvas(theme=theme)

# back to the built-in defaults
Config.reset()

Arguments passed to a method still win over the file: with the settings above, add_budget(..., stroke=Stroke(width=1)) draws a 1 pt line in the file's style.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
utility-viz init writes a commented template that lists every setting name, and utility-viz plot reads the same file with --config:

uv run utility-viz init                       # writes utility-viz.toml
uv run utility-viz plot --model cobb-douglas --px 2 --py 3 --income 30 \
    --config utility-viz.toml --output cd.png

docs.title: Figures & Demand Diagrams
docs.text:
utility-viz now includes higher-level teaching primitives on top of Canvas:

Tool Use it for Figure Multi-panel layouts PricePath, IncomePath Budget / equilibrium sweeps DemandDiagram Linked goods-space and Marshallian-demand views decompose_price_effect(...) Hicks and Slutsky decomposition EdgeworthBox Two-consumer exchange diagrams

docs.title: Multi-panel figures
docs.text:
Use Figure when one panel is not enough: before/after comparisons, decomposition diagrams, or classroom slides.

from utility_viz import Figure, Layout, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas

fig = Figure(
    Layout.SIDE_BY_SIDE,
    x_max=20,
    y_max=15,
    x_label="x",
    y_label="y",
    title="Before / After Price Change",
    shared_y=True,
)

cases = [
    (
        CobbDouglas(alpha=0.5, beta=0.5),
        2.0,
        3.0,
        30.0,
        r"Before: $p_x=2$",
    ),
    (
        CobbDouglas(alpha=0.3, beta=0.7),
        4.0,
        3.0,
        30.0,
        r"After: $p_x=4$",
    ),
]

for idx, (model, px, py, income, title) in enumerate(cases):
    eq = solve(model, px=px, py=py, income=income)
    panel = fig[idx]
    panel.ax.set_title(title)
    panel.add_utility(
        model, levels=levels.around(eq.utility, n=5), label="IC"
    )
    panel.add_budget(px, py, income, fill=True, label="BC")
    panel.add_equilibrium(eq, show_ray=True)

fig[0].show_legend(loc="upper right")
fig.save("figure_side_by_side.png")

docs.title: Available layouts
docs.text:
Figure supports these layouts:

Layout Panels Arrangement Layout.SINGLE 1 One full-size panel Layout.STACKED 2 Two panels, one above the other Layout.SIDE_BY_SIDE 2 Two panels, left and right Layout.TOP_TWO_BOTTOM_ONE 3 Two panels on top, one below Layout.TOP_ONE_BOTTOM_TWO 3 One panel on top, two below Layout.GRID_2X2 4 2 × 2 grid Layout.GRID_3X3 9 3 × 3 grid

Figure[idx] returns a panel Canvas, so the drawing API is the same once the layout exists.

docs.title: Path helpers
docs.text:
Path objects sweep one budget parameter while repeatedly solving the consumer problem.

from utility_viz import IncomePath, LinearBudget, PricePath
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas

model = CobbDouglas(alpha=0.5, beta=0.5)
budget = LinearBudget(px=2.0, py=2.0, income=40.0)

price_path = PricePath(
    model,
    budget=budget,
    price="px",
    price_range=(0.8, 6.0),
    n=40,
)
income_path = IncomePath(
    model,
    budget=budget,
    income_range=(20.0, 80.0),
    n=30,
)

Use these paths to:

  • draw PCC / ICC style equilibrium traces with Canvas.add_path(...)
  • feed a DemandDiagram
  • inspect how bundles move as prices or income vary

docs.title: Demand diagrams
docs.text:
DemandDiagram builds a stacked two-panel figure:

  • top panel: indifference curves, budget lines, equilibrium markers
  • bottom panel: the corresponding Marshallian demand curve
from utility_viz import DemandDiagram, LinearBudget, PricePath
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas

model = CobbDouglas(alpha=0.5, beta=0.5)
budget = LinearBudget(px=2.0, py=2.0, income=40.0)
path = PricePath(
    model,
    budget=budget,
    price="px",
    price_range=(0.8, 6.0),
    n=40,
)

fig = DemandDiagram(path, title="Demand: Cobb-Douglas")
fig.add_marshallian_panel(
    price_markers=[1.5, 4.0],
    show_pcc=False,
    show_demand_guides=True,
)
fig.save("demand_cobb_douglas.png")

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Keep these constraints in mind when building demand diagrams:

  • DemandDiagram currently expects a PricePath
  • it handles smooth, kinked, and corner-demand cases differently so the bottom panel stays economically meaningful
  • show_pcc=True overlays the price-consumption curve in the goods-space panel

docs.title: Price-effect decomposition
docs.text:
decompose_price_effect(...) separates a price change into substitution and income effects. Choose HICKS to hold the original utility fixed or SLUTSKY to keep the original bundle affordable.

from utility_viz import Canvas, DecompositionMethod, levels
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas
from utility_viz.optimizer import decompose_price_effect

model = CobbDouglas(alpha=0.5, beta=0.5)
result = decompose_price_effect(
    model,
    px=(2.0, 4.0),
    py=3.0,
    income=60.0,
    method=DecompositionMethod.HICKS,
)

(
    Canvas(x_max=25, y_max=25, title="Hicks decomposition")
    .add_decomposition(
        result,
        show_arrows=True,
        label_effects=True,
        show_x_projections=True,
    )
    .save("hicks.png")
)

add_decomposition draws the indifference curves through A and C by default, plus the one through B under Slutsky, where B is off the original curve. Pass show_curves=False when you draw them yourself with add_utility.

result.A, result.B, and result.C are the original, compensated, and final bundles. The result also exposes substitution_effect, income_effect, total_effect, and compensated_income.

Use Effect to set each effect's colour, the height of its range arrow below the axis, and a label beside it. point_label moves or hides the A, B, and C labels:

from utility_viz import Effect, Label

canvas.add_decomposition(
    result,
    substitution=Effect(
        color="#E67E22", label="SE", label_position="top"
    ),
    income=Effect(color="#27AE60", label="IE"),
    point_label=Label(visible=False),
)

curve_stroke and curve_label restyle and label those curves, and legend places the legend:

from utility_viz import Label, Legend, Stroke

canvas.add_decomposition(
    result,
    # restyle U0, U1 (and U_B)
    curve_stroke=Stroke(opacity=0.6),
    # turn on the U0, U1 labels
    curve_label=Label(position="top"),
    # or Legend(visible=False)
    legend=Legend(position="bottom"),
)

docs.title: Edgeworth box
docs.text:
EdgeworthBox draws a two-consumer exchange economy. Consumer A is measured from the lower-left origin, while consumer B is measured from the upper-right origin.

from utility_viz import EdgeworthBox
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas

box = EdgeworthBox(
    CobbDouglas(alpha=0.8, beta=0.2),
    CobbDouglas(alpha=0.2, beta=0.8),
    total_x=12.0,
    total_y=10.0,
    title="Asymmetric Cobb-Douglas",
)

(
    box.add_endowment(5.0, 4.0)
    .add_contract_curve(n=100, method="mrs")
    .add_core()
    .add_price_line(px=1.2, py=1.0)
    .add_walrasian_equilibrium(px=1.2, py=1.0)
    .show_legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5))
    .save("edgeworth.png")
)

Use method="mrs" for smooth preferences. Use method="pareto" for models with kinks, corners, or custom piecewise utility functions.

docs.title: Draw paths
docs.text:
When you do not need a full demand diagram, you can still render a path directly on a Canvas.

from utility_viz import Canvas, levels

eq = price_path.equilibria[len(price_path.equilibria) // 2]
lvls = levels.around(eq.utility, n=5)

Canvas(x_max=25, y_max=20).add_utility(
    model, levels=lvls
).add_path(price_path, label="PCC").save("price_path.png")

docs.title: Raster formats
docs.text:
Call cvs.save() with a .png, .pdf, or .svg extension:

# PNG, canvas DPI (default 300)
cvs.save("figure.png")
# PDF (vector)
cvs.save("figure.pdf")
# SVG (vector)
cvs.save("figure.svg")

The dpi parameter on Canvas controls raster resolution:

# lower DPI, faster preview
cvs = Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, dpi=150)

DPI is clamped to the range 1–1200.

docs.title: Animated GIF export
docs.text:
For multi-frame output, use Animator instead of Canvas.save():

from utility_viz.animation import Animator

Animator(draw_frame, frames=frames).save(
    "animation.gif", fps=12, dpi=120
)

See the Animation page for parameter, price, income, and budget-only sweep examples.

docs.title: Interactive window
docs.text:
Call cvs.show() to open a live matplotlib window instead of saving:

cvs.show()

In the CLI, omit --output to get the same behaviour:

utility-viz plot --model cobb-douglas --px 2 --py 3 --income 30

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text: WidgetViewer renders an utility-viz figure inside a notebook cell and redraws it whenever a control changes. Every parameter gets both a slider and a numeric input box, so users can drag for intuition or type exact values for teaching and demos.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
uv add "utility-viz[interactive]"

If you also want GIF export:

uv add "utility-viz[all]"

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
from utility_viz import Canvas, levels, solve
from utility_viz.interactive import WidgetViewer
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas


def draw(alpha: float, px: float) -> Canvas:
    model = CobbDouglas(alpha=alpha, beta=1.0 - alpha)
    eq = solve(model, px=px, py=2.0, income=20.0)

    return (
        Canvas(
            x_max=14,
            y_max=12,
            x_label="X_1",
            y_label="X_2",
            title="Interactive equilibrium",
        )
        .add_utility(
            model, levels=levels.around(eq.utility, n=5)
        )
        .add_budget(px=px, py=2.0, income=20.0, fill=True)
        .add_equilibrium(eq, show_ray=True, drop_dashes=True)
    )


WidgetViewer(
    draw,
    alpha=(0.2, 0.8, 0.05),
    px=(1.0, 6.0, 0.25),
).show()

docs.title: Widget behavior
docs.text:
The widget layer handles these interactions automatically:

  • Builds one FloatSlider per parameter.
  • Builds one linked FloatText input per parameter.
  • Keeps slider and typed values in sync.
  • Clears the old figure before redrawing, so notebook cells do not accumulate a stack of stale plots.

docs.title: Notebook setup
docs.text:
For fresh notebook runtimes, especially in Colab:

  1. Run the install cell once.
  2. Restart the runtime once if ipywidgets, traitlets, or IPython were upgraded.
  3. Skip the install cell after restart and continue from the import cell.

The packaged Playground notebook now follows this flow and avoids reinstalling when utility-viz is already installed.

docs.title: Widgets or GIFs
docs.text:
Choose the output that fits the teaching setting:

Tool Use it when WidgetViewer Students need to type or drag parameters and inspect one state at a time Animator You want a fixed, repeatable narrative sweep for slides, docs, or the project website

docs.title: Themes
docs.text: Themes control all colours and stroke widths used by the Canvas.

docs.title: Default
docs.text:
from utility_viz import Canvas, themes

cvs = Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, theme=themes.default)

The default theme draws from a colour-blind-friendly colour cycle (thriveth, 2014), exposed as themes.COLORBLIND_CYCLE_HEX and themes.COLORBLIND_CYCLE_RGB. Economics teaching relies heavily on graphs, so colour alone should not carry meaning for students with impaired vision (Kugler & Andrews, 1996).

docs.title: Nord
docs.text:
cvs = Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, theme=themes.nord)

The Nord theme uses the Nord colour palette — cool blues and muted tones suitable for academic presentations.

docs.title: Paper
docs.text:
cvs = Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, theme=themes.paper)

The paper theme uses thinner lines, smaller markers, and restrained typography on a transparent background — suitable for print and journal figures where ink and space are at a premium.

docs.title: Monochrome
docs.text:
cvs = Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, theme=themes.monochrome)

The monochrome theme drops colour entirely — every element is a shade of gray — and instead distinguishes curves, budget lines, and rays by line style, and markers by shape. Suitable for black-and-white printing or figures viewed by colour-blind readers without relying on colour at all.

docs.title: Presentation
docs.text:
cvs = Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, theme=themes.presentation)

The presentation theme uses larger text, thicker lines, and bigger markers for visibility on a projector screen or in a lecture hall.

docs.title: Dark
docs.text:
cvs = Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, theme=themes.dark)

The dark theme uses a dark background with light foreground colours, suitable for dark-mode slides or websites.

docs.title: Custom theme
docs.text:
Pass any field to the constructor to override just that value; everything else keeps the built-in default:

from utility_viz import Theme

my_theme = Theme(
    name="custom",
    axis_color="#333333",
    label_color="#333333",
    ic_color="#2563eb",
    ic_linewidth=1.5,
    budget_color="#dc2626",
    eq_color="#16a34a",
    eq_markersize=6.0,
)

cvs = Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, theme=my_theme)

Every line, marker, fill, label, and legend a diagram draws also has a composite default -- theme.ic_stroke, theme.eq_marker, theme.point_label, and so on -- built from the fields above. To change one of these as a whole (for example, giving the core segment of an Edgeworth box its own arrowhead, not just its own colour), subclass Theme and override the property:

from utility_viz import ArrowStyle, Stroke, Theme


class MyTheme(Theme):
    @property
    def core_stroke(self) -> Stroke:
        return Stroke(
            width=3.0,
            color="#C0392B",
            arrow=ArrowStyle.TRIANGLE,
        )


cvs = EdgeworthBox(..., theme=MyTheme(name="my-theme"))

Passing an explicit argument to a method (add_core(stroke=...)) still wins over the theme, and the theme still wins over the built-in default -- the same precedence a settings file follows.

docs.text:

Budget-line stroke colour and width

Opacity of the feasible-set shading

Equilibrium marker colour and size

Expansion-path ray colour and width

Kink-point marker colour

Substitution- / income-effect arrow colours

Effect-arrow width

Compensated budget line in a decomposition

docs.title: Style properties
docs.text:
Every property below is a Stroke, Marker, Label, Fill, or Legend, built from the fields above. Overriding one in a subclass changes every diagram that doesn't pass its own explicit argument for that role; the settings file sets the same properties from [stroke.<name>], [marker.<name>], [label.<name>], and [fill.<name>] sections.

Stroke

ic_stroke, secondary_ic_stroke, budget_stroke, ray_stroke, path_stroke, compensated_budget_stroke, final_budget_stroke, substitution_stroke, income_stroke, subsistence_stroke, contract_stroke, core_stroke, price_stroke, axis_stroke, drop_stroke, projection_stroke, guide_stroke, box_stroke

Legend

docs.title: Core Models
docs.text: The core models cover smooth preferences, kinked and linear preferences, and preferences with income or reference-point effects. Choose a group, then switch between its tabs to compare models.

docs.title: Smooth preferences
docs.text:
These models produce smooth indifference curves and normally have an interior optimum when prices and income are positive.

Cobb-DouglasCESTranslog

Cobb-Douglas is the standard model for smooth, strictly convex preferences.

\[ U(x,y)=x^\alpha y^\beta \]

The exponents control the relative weight placed on each good. Its indifference curves approach both axes without touching them.

Parameters

alphaDefault: 0.5

Weight on good \(x\)

betaDefault: 0.5

Weight on good \(y\)

Example

from utility_viz import Canvas, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas

model = CobbDouglas(alpha=0.5, beta=0.5)
eq = solve(model, px=2.0, py=3.0, income=30.0)

(
    Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, title="Cobb-Douglas")
    .add_utility(model, levels=levels.around(eq.utility, n=5))
    .add_budget(2.0, 3.0, 30.0, fill=True)
    .add_equilibrium(eq, show_ray=True)
    .save("cobb_douglas.png")
)

CES lets the ease of substitution vary while keeping preferences smooth.

\[ U(x,y)=\left(\alpha x^\rho+\beta y^\rho\right)^{1/\rho} \]

The substitution elasticity is \(\sigma=1/(1-\rho)\). As \(\rho\) changes, CES approaches Cobb-Douglas, Leontief, or perfect substitutes.

Parameters

alphaDefault: 0.5

Weight on good \(x\)

betaDefault: 0.5

Weight on good \(y\)

rhoDefault: 0.5

Substitution parameter, with \(\rho\ne1\)

Example

from utility_viz import Canvas, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import CES

model = CES(alpha=0.5, beta=0.5, rho=-0.5)
eq = solve(model, px=2.0, py=3.0, income=30.0)

(
    Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, title="CES")
    .add_utility(model, levels=levels.around(eq.utility, n=5))
    .add_budget(2.0, 3.0, 30.0)
    .add_equilibrium(eq)
    .save("ces.png")
)

Translog is a flexible log-quadratic model for smooth preferences.

\[ \begin{aligned} \ln U(x,y)={}&\alpha_0+\alpha_x\ln x+\alpha_y\ln y\\ &+\tfrac12\beta_{xx}(\ln x)^2 +\tfrac12\beta_{yy}(\ln y)^2 +\beta_{xy}\ln x\ln y \end{aligned} \]

The quadratic and interaction terms allow curvature to vary across the consumption space. Setting all \(\beta\) coefficients to zero gives a Cobb-Douglas-style log-linear form.

Parameters

alpha_0Default: 0.0

Log-utility intercept

alpha_xDefault: 0.5

First-order weight on \(\ln x\)

alpha_yDefault: 0.5

First-order weight on \(\ln y\)

beta_xxDefault: 0.0

Curvature in \(x\)

beta_yyDefault: 0.0

Curvature in \(y\)

beta_xyDefault: 0.0

Interaction between \(x\) and \(y\)

Example

from utility_viz import Canvas, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import Translog

model = Translog(alpha_x=0.6, alpha_y=0.4, beta_xy=0.12)
eq = solve(model, px=2.0, py=3.0, income=30.0)

(
    Canvas(x_max=18, y_max=12, title="Translog")
    .add_utility(model, levels=levels.around(eq.utility, n=4))
    .add_budget(2.0, 3.0, 30.0)
    .add_equilibrium(eq)
    .save("translog.png")
)

docs.title: Kinks and corners
docs.text:
These models show how non-smooth or linear preferences change the location of the optimum.

LeontiefPerfect SubstitutesMaximum Utility

Leontief preferences describe goods consumed in fixed proportions.

\[ U(x,y)=\min(ax,by) \]

Indifference curves are L-shaped. The optimum lies at the kink where the two weighted quantities are equal.

Parameters

aDefault: 1.0

Weight on good \(x\)

bDefault: 1.0

Weight on good \(y\)

Example

from utility_viz import Canvas, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import Leontief

model = Leontief(a=1.0, b=1.0)
eq = solve(model, px=2.0, py=3.0, income=30.0)

(
    Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, title="Leontief")
    .add_utility(
        model,
        levels=levels.around(eq.utility, n=5),
        show_rays=True,
        show_kinks=True,
    )
    .add_budget(2.0, 3.0, 30.0)
    .add_equilibrium(eq)
    .save("leontief.png")
)

Perfect substitutes provide constant utility trade-offs between goods.

\[ U(x,y)=ax+by \]

Indifference curves are straight lines. The consumer normally chooses the good with the greater marginal utility per dollar, producing a corner solution.

Parameters

aDefault: 1.0

Marginal utility of good \(x\)

bDefault: 1.0

Marginal utility of good \(y\)

Example

from utility_viz import Canvas, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import PerfectSubstitutes

model = PerfectSubstitutes(a=1.0, b=2.0)
eq = solve(model, px=2.0, py=3.0, income=30.0)

(
    Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, title="Perfect Substitutes")
    .add_utility(model, levels=levels.around(eq.utility, n=5))
    .add_budget(2.0, 3.0, 30.0)
    .add_equilibrium(eq)
    .save("perfect_substitutes.png")
)

Maximum utility keeps only the larger weighted quantity in each bundle.

\[ U(x,y)=\max(ax,by) \]

Each indifference curve has two arms that extend toward the axes. The resulting preferences are non-convex, so the optimum on a linear budget normally lies at the intercept with the greater weighted utility.

Parameters

aDefault: 1.0

Weight on good \(x\)

bDefault: 1.0

Weight on good \(y\)

Example

import numpy as np
from utility_viz import Canvas, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import CustomUtility

a, b = 1.0, 1.0
model = CustomUtility(
    func=lambda x, y: np.maximum(a * x, b * y),
    name="maximum",
)
eq = solve(model, px=2.0, py=3.0, income=30.0)

(
    Canvas(x_max=25, y_max=20, title="Maximum utility")
    .add_utility(model, levels=levels.around(eq.utility, n=5))
    .add_budget(2.0, 3.0, 30.0)
    .add_equilibrium(eq)
    .save("maximum.png")
)

docs.title: Income and reference points
docs.text:
These models add special income effects, subsistence requirements, or a preferred consumption point.

Quasi-LinearStone-GearySatiation

Quasi-linear preferences place one good linearly in utility.

\[ U(x,y)=f(x)+y \]

The non-linear good has no income effect once the solution is interior. linear_in can reverse the roles of \(x\) and \(y\).

Parameters

v_funcDefault: numpy.log

Increasing, concave function \(f\)

linear_inDefault: "y"

Good that enters linearly

Example

import numpy as np
from utility_viz import Canvas, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import QuasiLinear

model = QuasiLinear(v_func=np.log, linear_in="y")
eq = solve(model, px=2.0, py=1.0, income=20.0)

(
    Canvas(x_max=15, y_max=15, title="Quasi-Linear")
    .add_utility(model, levels=levels.around(eq.utility, n=5))
    .add_budget(2.0, 1.0, 20.0)
    .add_equilibrium(eq)
    .save("quasi_linear.png")
)

Stone-Geary extends Cobb-Douglas with minimum consumption requirements.

\[ U(x,y)=(x-\bar{x})^\alpha(y-\bar{y})^\beta \]

The consumer first covers subsistence quantities \(\bar{x}\) and \(\bar{y}\), then allocates the remaining income like a Cobb-Douglas consumer.

Parameters

alphaDefault: 0.5

Weight on supernumerary \(x\)

betaDefault: 0.5

Weight on supernumerary \(y\)

bar_xDefault: 1.0

Subsistence quantity \(\bar{x}\)

bar_yDefault: 1.0

Subsistence quantity \(\bar{y}\)

Example

from utility_viz import Canvas, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import StoneGeary

model = StoneGeary(alpha=0.5, beta=0.5, bar_x=2.0, bar_y=2.0)
eq = solve(model, px=2.0, py=3.0, income=30.0)

(
    Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, title="Stone-Geary")
    .add_utility(model, levels=levels.around(eq.utility, n=5))
    .add_budget(2.0, 3.0, 30.0, fill=True)
    .add_equilibrium(eq)
    .save("stone_geary.png")
)

Satiation preferences have a bliss point that maximises utility.

\[ U(x,y)=-a(x-x^*)^2-b(y-y^*)^2 \]

Utility falls in every direction away from \((x^*,y^*)\), so indifference curves form closed ellipses and monotonicity does not hold.

Parameters

bliss_xDefault: 5.0

Bliss-point coordinate \(x^*\)

bliss_yDefault: 5.0

Bliss-point coordinate \(y^*\)

aDefault: 1.0

Curvature along the \(x\)-axis

bDefault: 1.0

Curvature along the \(y\)-axis

Example

import numpy as np
from utility_viz import Canvas, levels
from utility_viz.models import Satiation

model = Satiation(bliss_x=6.0, bliss_y=4.0)
x = np.linspace(0.1, 12.0, 300)
y = np.linspace(0.1, 10.0, 300)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)

(
    Canvas(x_max=12, y_max=10, title="Satiation")
    .add_utility(
        model, levels=levels.percentile(model(X, Y), n=5)
    )
    .save("satiation.png")
)

For custom functions and multi-good Cobb-Douglas models, see Advanced Models.

docs.title: Advanced Models
docs.text: Advanced models extend the built-in utility families with user-defined functions, more than two goods, or goods that are inferior or Giffen.

docs.title: Extensible models
docs.text:
Use these models when a predefined two-good utility class is not enough.

Custom UtilityMulti-Good Cobb-Douglas

CustomUtility wraps any vectorised Python callable as an utility-viz model.

\[ U(x,y)=\ln x+\ln y \]

The equation above is one example. The callable must accept two NumPy arrays and return an array with the same shape.

Parameters

func

Vectorised utility function of \(x\) and \(y\)

name

Display name for the custom model

Example

import numpy as np
from utility_viz import Canvas, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import CustomUtility

model = CustomUtility(
    func=lambda x, y: np.log(x) + np.log(y),
    name="log+log",
)
eq = solve(model, px=2.0, py=3.0, income=30.0)

(
    Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, title="Custom Utility")
    .add_utility(model, levels=levels.around(eq.utility, n=5))
    .add_budget(2.0, 3.0, 30.0)
    .add_equilibrium(eq)
    .save("custom.png")
)

MultiGoodCD represents Cobb-Douglas preferences over \(N\) goods.

\[ U(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}x_i^{\alpha_i} \]

freeze() fixes every good except \(x\) and \(y\), then returns a CustomUtility that can be drawn on a two-dimensional canvas.

Parameters

shares

Mapping from each good name to its exponent \(\alpha_i\)

freeze(...)

Fixed quantities for goods other than \(x\) and \(y\)

Example

from utility_viz import Canvas, levels, solve
from utility_viz.models import MultiGoodCD

model = MultiGoodCD({"x": 0.3, "y": 0.3, "z": 0.4})
two_good_model = model.freeze(z=10.0)
eq = solve(two_good_model, px=2.0, py=3.0, income=30.0)

(
    Canvas(x_max=20, y_max=15, title="Multi-Good Cobb-Douglas")
    .add_utility(
        two_good_model,
        levels=levels.around(eq.utility, n=5),
    )
    .add_budget(2.0, 3.0, 30.0, fill=True)
    .add_equilibrium(eq)
    .save("multigood.png")
)

docs.title: Inferior and Giffen goods
docs.text:
Haagsma implements the utility function of Haagsma(2012), in which good \(x\) is always inferior and becomes a Giffen good when income is high enough.

\[ U(x,y)=\alpha_x\ln(x-\gamma_x)-\alpha_y\ln(\gamma_y-y), \qquad 0<\alpha_x<\alpha_y,\quad x>\gamma_x,\quad 0\le y<\gamma_y \]

At an interior optimum, Marshallian demand for \(x\) has a closed form:

\[ x^*=\frac{\alpha_x(\gamma_y p_y-I)}{(\alpha_y-\alpha_x)\,p_x}+\frac{\alpha_y\gamma_x}{\alpha_y-\alpha_x} \]

so \(\partial x^*/\partial I<0\) for every price and income. The sign of \(\partial x^*/\partial p_x\) depends on income:

Income Good \(x\) \(I<\gamma_y p_y\) Inferior; demand still falls as \(p_x\) rises \(I=\gamma_y p_y\) Inferior; substitution and income effects cancel \(\gamma_y p_y<I<\gamma_y p_y+\gamma_x p_x\) Giffen; demand rises with \(p_x\)

With \(I\ge\gamma_y p_y+\gamma_x p_x\) the consumer can push \(y\) towards \(\gamma_y\), utility grows without bound, and no optimum exists; solve() raises an error.

Parameters

alpha_x

Weight \(\alpha_x\) on good \(x\), below alpha_y

alpha_y

Weight \(\alpha_y\) on good \(y\)

gamma_x

Lower bound \(\gamma_x\) of good \(x\)

gamma_y

Upper bound \(\gamma_y\) of good \(y\)

demand(px, py, income) returns the closed-form bundle, and is_giffen(px, py, income) reports whether \(x\) is a Giffen good.

Example

from utility_viz import Canvas, Effect
from utility_viz.models import Haagsma
from utility_viz.optimizer import decompose_price_effect

model = Haagsma(
    alpha_x=1.0, alpha_y=2.0, gamma_x=2.0, gamma_y=27.0
)
# True
model.is_giffen(px=2.0, py=1.0, income=28.0)

result = decompose_price_effect(
    model, px=(2.0, 1.0), py=1.0, income=28.0, method="hicks"
)

(
    Canvas(x_max=16, y_max=32, title="Haagsma: Giffen good")
    .add_decomposition(
        result,
        show_x_projections=True,
        substitution=Effect(label="SE"),
        income=Effect(label="IE"),
    )
    .save("haagsma.png")
)

When \(p_x\) falls from 2 to 1, the substitution effect raises \(x\) by 4.5 while the income effect lowers it by 5, so demand for \(x\) falls.

Release history of utility-viz, formerly econ-viz. Documentation-only changes are not listed.

v1.11.02026-09-26

Maintenance

v1.9.02026-09-26

Features

  • Price-effect decompositions draw their indifference curves by default: $U_0$ through A, $U_1$ through C, and the curve through B under Slutsky
  • Haagsma utility model with an always-inferior good that becomes Giffen at high enough income
  • Legend placed automatically where it covers the least of the diagram, or at a chosen corner or side

  • opacity on Stroke, Marker, Label, Legend, Effect, and Fill

Changes

  • Existing decomposition figures now include their indifference curves; show_curves=False restores the previous figure
  • Effect range arrows point one way, from A to B and from B to C

Bug fixes

  • Tighter optimisation tolerance, so comparative statics and Slutsky matrices are accurate
  • Indifference curves at negative utility levels are drawn solid
v1.8.02026-09-26

Features

  • Effect sets the colour, range-arrow height, and label of each price-effect decomposition effect
  • Marker sets point colour, size, and shape across canvases, demand diagrams, and Edgeworth boxes
  • Label sets point-label text, position (four sides and four corners), offset, colour, size, and visibility; decomposition A/B/C labels can be hidden

Bug fixes

  • Per-figure text and math fonts without changing Matplotlib's global configuration
  • Stroke controls line width, style, colour, and arrowheads across canvases, figures, demand diagrams, and Edgeworth boxes

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: utility-viz now includes analysis helpers beyond plotting and equilibrium solving.

docs.title: Comparative statics
docs.text:
Use comparative_statics(...) to estimate the six Marshallian demand derivatives numerically:

from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas
from utility_viz.optimizer import comparative_statics

model = CobbDouglas(alpha=0.4, beta=0.6)
cs = comparative_statics(model, px=2.0, py=3.0, income=60.0)

print(
    round(cs.dx_dpx, 1), round(cs.dx_dpy, 1), round(cs.dx_dI, 1)
)
print(
    round(cs.dy_dpx, 1), round(cs.dy_dpy, 1), round(cs.dy_dI, 1)
)

# -6.0 0.0 0.2
# 0.0 -4.0 0.2

Notes:

  • Uses central finite differences around solve(...)
  • Default relative step size is 1e-3
  • Emits warnings for economically unusual sign patterns such as Giffen-style own-price responses or inferior-good income effects

docs.title: Slutsky matrix
docs.text:
Use slutsky_matrix(...) to compute the two-good substitution matrix implied by the Slutsky equation.

from utility_viz import slutsky_matrix
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas

S = slutsky_matrix(
    CobbDouglas(alpha=0.4, beta=0.6),
    px=2.0,
    py=3.0,
    income=60.0,
)

print(round(S.s_xx, 1), round(S.s_xy, 1))
print(round(S.s_yx, 1), round(S.s_yy, 1))
print(S.as_array().round(1))

# -3.6 2.4
# 2.4 -1.6
# [[-3.6  2.4]
#  [ 2.4 -1.6]]

Use this when you want compensated price effects rather than just the raw Marshallian derivatives.

docs.title: Homogeneity analysis
docs.text: Use HomogeneityAnalyzer to study whether a utility function is homogeneous or homothetic.

docs.title: Available checks
docs.text:
The analyzer provides four checks:

degree()

Estimates the homogeneity degree

euler_check(x, y)

Evaluates the Euler-theorem residual at a bundle

is_homothetic()

Whether MRS is invariant to proportional scaling

demand_degree_zero(px, py, income)

Whether Marshallian demand is homogeneous of degree 0

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from utility_viz.analysis import HomogeneityAnalyzer
from utility_viz.models import CobbDouglas

analyzer = HomogeneityAnalyzer(CobbDouglas(alpha=0.4, beta=0.6))
result = analyzer.degree()

print(round(result.degree, 6))
print(result.returns_to_scale)
print(round(analyzer.euler_check(3.0, 4.0), 6))
print(analyzer.is_homothetic())
print(analyzer.demand_degree_zero(px=2.0, py=3.0, income=60.0))

# 1.0
# ReturnsToScale.CONSTANT
# 0.0
# True
# True

docs.title: Returns to scale
docs.text:
degree() returns a HomogeneityResult carrying both the estimated degree and a ReturnsToScale classification:

For a Cobb–Douglas utility, the degree is \(\alpha+\beta\):

\[ U(\lambda x, \lambda y) = \lambda^{\alpha+\beta} U(x,y) \]
  • \(\alpha+\beta>1\): INCREASING
  • \(\alpha+\beta=1\): CONSTANT
  • \(\alpha+\beta<1\): DECREASING

Functions without a consistent homogeneity degree are classified as NOT_HOMOGENEOUS.

docs.title: Classification example
docs.text:
def shifted_utility(x, y):
    return x**0.4 * y**0.6 + 1.0


models = [
    CobbDouglas(alpha=0.7, beta=0.6),
    CobbDouglas(alpha=0.4, beta=0.6),
    CobbDouglas(alpha=0.2, beta=0.5),
    shifted_utility,
]

for model in models:
    result = HomogeneityAnalyzer(model).degree()
    degree = (
        None
        if result.degree is None
        else round(result.degree, 1)
    )
    print(degree, result.returns_to_scale.name)

# 1.3 INCREASING
# 1.0 CONSTANT
# 0.7 DECREASING
# None NOT_HOMOGENEOUS

docs.title: Equilibrium solver
docs.text:
Find the utility-maximizing bundle under a linear budget constraint.

solve(
    func: UtilityFunction,
    px: float,
    py: float,
    income: float,
) → Equilibrium
funcUtilityFunctionRequired

Utility model to maximize.

pxfloatRequired

Positive price of good X.

pyfloatRequired

Positive price of good Y.

incomefloatRequired

Positive total budget.

docs.title: Utility levels
docs.text:
levels provides utility levels for indifference curves: around centers them on a reference value; percentile selects them from a utility surface.

levels.around(
    anchor: float,
    n: int,
    spread: float,
) → list[float]
anchorfloatRequired

Reference utility level.

nintDefault: 5

Number of levels, at least one.

spreadfloatDefault: 0.5

Half-width as a fraction of the absolute anchor; zero uses unit scale.

levels.percentile(
    Z: ndarray,
    n: int,
    lo: float,
    hi: float,
) → list[float]
ZndarrayRequired

Two-dimensional utility values.

nintDefault: 5

Number of levels.

lofloatDefault: 20

Lower percentile, from 0 to 100.

hifloatDefault: 80

Upper percentile, from 0 to 100.

docs.title: LaTeX Parsing
docs.text:
parse_latex converts a LaTeX math string directly into a concrete model instance.

from utility_viz import parse_latex

# CobbDouglas(alpha=0.4, beta=0.6)
model = parse_latex(r"x^{0.4} y^{0.6}")
# Leontief(a=2.0, b=3.0)
model = parse_latex(r"\min(2x, 3y)")
# PerfectSubstitutes(a=2.0, b=3.0)
model = parse_latex(r"2x + 3y")

docs.title: Supported forms
docs.text:
Family Pattern Example Cobb-Douglas x^{α} y^{β} or x^α y^β x^{0.3} y^{0.7} Leontief \min(ax, by) or min(ax, by) \min(2x, y) Perfect Substitutes ax + by 3x + 1.5y

Coefficients and exponents are optional and default to 1.

docs.title: Input forms
docs.text:
Enter the utility expression alone, or prefix it with U = or U(x, y) =:

U(x,y) = x^{0.5} y^{0.5}
U = x^{0.5} y^{0.5}
x^{0.5} y^{0.5}

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Unrecognised patterns raise utility_viz.exceptions.ParseError:

from utility_viz.exceptions import ParseError

try:
    model = parse_latex(r"x^2 + y^2")
except ParseError as e:
    print(e)

# Unrecognised LaTeX utility function: 'x^2 + y^2'
# Supported forms:
#   Cobb-Douglas       : x^{alpha} y^{beta}
#   Leontief           : \min(ax, by)
#   Perfect Substitutes: ax + by
#   CES                : (alpha x^{rho} + beta y^{rho})^{1/rho}

docs.title: In the CLI
docs.text: utility-viz plot --latex "x^{0.4} y^{0.6}" --px 2 --py 3 --income 30 -o out.png

docs.title: 模組
docs.text: EconViz 由四個套件組成：兩個負責繪製經濟學圖形，另外兩個是它們共用的通用元件。

docs.title: 經濟學套件
docs.text:
兩個負責繪製經濟學圖形的套件。

  • utility-viz

    繪製出版品質的個體經濟學圖形：無異曲線、預算限制、消費者均衡，並可匯出 TikZ。

    uv add --prerelease allow utility-viz

    2.0 版目前為 Beta。

    utility-viz

  • principle-viz

    經濟學原理的市場分析與圖形：均衡、租稅、價格管制、福利與貿易，以線性需求與供給為基礎。

    uv add principle-viz

    principle-viz

docs.title: 底層套件
docs.text:
兩個通用的基礎元件，由經濟學套件共用。

  • mosaickit

    與領域無關的工具組，用場景、圖層、樣式、參數與渲染器組合出二維圖形。

    uv add mosaickit

    mosaickit

  • bezierkit

    小巧的數學工具組，用來建構、分析與匯出貝茲曲線，並原生支援 SVG 與 TikZ 輸出。

    uv add bezierkit

    目前的穩定版本為 1.0.1。

    bezierkit

docs.title: 總覽
docs.text:
bezierkit：Python 貝茲曲線工具組

小巧且與渲染器無關的貝茲曲線 Python 工具組。

from bezierkit import BezierCurve, Point
from bezierkit.sampling import UniformSampler

curve = BezierCurve.cubic(
    Point(0, 0),
    Point(1, 2),
    Point(3, 2),
    Point(4, 0),
)

# Point(coords=(2.0, 1.5))
print(curve.at(0.5))

# cut the curve in two
left, right = curve.split(0.3)

sample = UniformSampler(200).sample(curve)
print(len(sample.points), "sample points")

docs.title: 功能特色
docs.text:
• 任意次數的曲線

    BezierCurve、CubicBezierSegment 與 PiecewiseBezier，搭配不可變的 Point、Vector 與 PointSet 值物件。

    Bézier 曲線

  • 求值與分割

    以 de Casteljau 演算法求值，並對曲線求導、分割、截取與反轉。

    導數、分割與反轉

  • 由斜率建構

    用 PlanarSlopes 由端點與端點斜率建構三次曲線，或由 Hermite 資料建構。

    建構與 Hermite 插值

  • 擬合與等值線

    函數圖形的自適應擬合與實測誤差、折線簡化，以及隱函數等值線的描繪。

    擬合

  • 原生匯出

    具版本的 JSON 格式、SVG 三次路徑資料與 TikZ controls 指令，不會攤平成折線。

    取樣與匯出

  • 選用功能

    Matplotlib 路徑轉接器與命令列工具。

    命令列

docs.title: 數學與證明
docs.text:
指南把演算法所依據的性質寫成定理：Bernstein 基底的保證、de Casteljau 演算法為何能求值並分割曲線、Hermite 插值最多偏離多少，以及匯出器因四捨五入損失多少精度。每個證明都摺疊在定理下方，點開才會展開，因此頁面平常讀起來就是 API 文件。標準參考書為 Farin (2002) 與 Prautzsch 等人 (2002)，見參考文獻。

符號

點位於某個維度 \(d \ge 1\) 的 \(\mathbb{R}^d\) 中；多數圖使用 \(d = 2\)。\(n\) 次 Bézier 曲線有 \(n + 1\) 個控制點 \(P_0, \dots, P_n\)，定義為映射

\[ B(t) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} b_{i,n}(t)\, P_i, \qquad t \in [0, 1], \]

其中 \(b_{i,n}(t) = \binom{n}{i} t^i (1-t)^{n-i}\) 為 Bernstein 多項式。套件中每條曲線的參數範圍都是 \([0, 1]\)； 超出範圍的參數會拋出 ParameterOutOfDomain。

docs.title: 閱讀指引
docs.text:
主題 頁面 點、向量、參數、例外 幾何數值物件 Bernstein 基底、曲線、求值 Bézier 曲線 導數、分割、反轉 導數、分割與反轉 三次線段與分段路徑 三次線段與路徑 建構與 Hermite 插值 建構與 Hermite 插值 擬合函數與折線 擬合 描繪等值線 等值線 取樣、JSON、SVG、TikZ、Matplotlib 取樣與匯出 命令列 命令列

初次使用時，先讀快速開始與 Bézier 曲線。

範圍

繪圖樣式與圖形語意刻意不在這個套件的範圍內：它本身不繪圖。交點、B 樣條與 NURBS 屬於未來的工作。

docs.title: 安裝
docs.text:
uv add bezierkit

需要 Python 3.10 以上。選用功能與開發環境請見安裝，或直接看快速入門。

docs.title: 命令列介面
docs.text:
安裝 cli 選用依賴後即可使用 bezierkit 指令，在命令列計算、取樣與建構曲線。預設輸出表格，也可輸出 JSON 或 CSV 給其他程式使用。

bezierkit evaluate --points "0,0" --points "1,2" --points "3,2" --points "4,0" \
                   --t 0.5 --order 1 --json
# [{"t":0.5,"value":[4.5,0.0]}]

docs.title: 控制點
docs.text: 需要曲線的指令以重複的 --points 選項接收控制點，每個是以逗號分隔的座標（"1,2"，三維則為 "1,2,3"）。省略 --points 時，指令從標準輸入讀取含 control_points 陣列的 JSON 物件，也就是 construct 的輸出，因此指令之間可以用管線串接。

docs.title: 指令
docs.text:
bezierkit evaluate --t values [--points ...] [--order int] [--json]

在每個 --t 計算曲線值，或其 --order 階導數（預設 0）。每個值可為數字或含端點的範圍 start:stop:step，例如 0:1:0.25；--t 可重複。

bezierkit sample [--points ...] [--count int] [--format table|csv|json] [--output path]

以 --count 個（預設 50）等距參數取樣，含兩端，每列為 t、x、y（三維另有 z，更高維為 c3、c4……）。--output 寫入檔案而非標準輸出。

bezierkit construct slopes --start point --end point --start-slope float --end-slope float [--start-handle --end-handle]
bezierkit construct tangents --start ... --end ... --start-direction vector --end-direction vector [...]

以 PlanarSlopes 或 TangentDirections（詳見建構與 Hermite 插值）建構三次曲線，並以 JSON 印出控制點。

bezierkit construct slopes --start "0,5" --end "5,0" \
                           --start-slope -2 --end-slope -0.3 \
| bezierkit sample --count 3 --format csv
# t,x,y
# 0.0,0.0,5.0
# 0.5,2.3085202413545525,2.272345260462411
# 1.0,5.0,0.0

docs.title: 錯誤
docs.text: 無效輸入（例如格式錯誤的點，或超出 \([0, 1]\) 的參數）會在標準錯誤輸出印出 Error: ...，結束狀態為 1，不顯示 traceback。在指令前加上全域選項 --debug 可改為顯示 Python traceback。

docs.title: 系統需求
docs.text:
bezierkit 需要 Python 3.10 以上版本與 NumPy。另有兩組選用依賴：

cli

bezierkit 指令（詳見命令列介面）；安裝 Typer 與 Rich。

matplotlib

與 Matplotlib Path 物件互相轉換（詳見Matplotlib）。

docs.title: 安裝套件
docs.text:
uv add bezierkit                 # the library
uv add "bezierkit[cli]"          # with the command-line interface
uv add "bezierkit[matplotlib]"   # with the Matplotlib adapter
uv add "bezierkit==1.0.0"        # the version this manual describes

使用 pip 時，執行 python -m pip install bezierkit，選用依賴的寫法相同。1.0.0 是第一個正式版：bezierkit 及其文件所列子套件匯出的名稱依語意化版本管理，JSON 路徑格式維持第 1 版。

docs.title: 開發環境設定
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/EconViz/bezierkit.git
cd bezierkit
uv sync --all-extras --dev
uv run pytest
uv run ruff check src tests benchmarks
uv run lint-imports

持續整合流程在 Python 3.10、3.11、3.12 與 3.13 上執行相同指令。lint-imports 檢查套件分層：數學核心不匯入任何繪圖端，只有轉接器匯入 Matplotlib。

docs.title: 一條三次曲線
docs.text:
本手冊通篇使用的曲線，是控制點為 \((0, 0)\)、\((1, 2)\)、\((3, 2)\)、\((4, 0)\) 的三次曲線（參見三次曲線及其控制凸包。）。

from bezierkit import BezierCurve, PiecewiseBezier, Point
from bezierkit.bezier import to_cubic
from bezierkit.export.tikz import to_tikz

curve = BezierCurve.cubic(
    Point(0, 0), Point(1, 2), Point(3, 2), Point(4, 0)
)
# Point(coords=(2.0, 1.5))
print(curve.at(0.5))
# Point(coords=(4.5, 0.0))
print(curve.derivative().at(0.5))
# two cubics that together trace curve
left, right = curve.split(0.4)

path = PiecewiseBezier([to_cubic(curve)])
print(to_tikz(path, precision=2, options="thick"))
# \draw[thick] (0.00,0.00) .. controls (1.00,2.00) and (3.00,2.00) .. (4.00,0.00);

曲線由 \(P_0\) 出發、在 \(P_3\) 結束，離開 \(P_0\) 時朝向 \(P_1\)，抵達 \(P_3\) 時來自 \(P_2\) 的方向，且始終位於控制點的凸包內（詳見凸包）。最後一行是這條曲線的 TikZ 路徑，可直接貼進 LaTeX 文件。

docs.title: 主要元件
docs.text:
• 數值物件。Point、Vector 與 PointSet 不可變，並檢查維度（詳見幾何數值物件）。
  • 曲線。BezierCurve 可為任意次數與維度；CubicBezierSegment 是繪圖端使用的三次曲線；PiecewiseBezier 將三次曲線連接成路徑（詳見Bézier 曲線、三次線段與路徑）。
  • 建構。把端點條件、斜率、導數或 Hermite 資料轉為控制點（詳見建構與 Hermite 插值）。
  • 近似。把平滑函數、取樣點與等值線 \(F(x, y) = c\) 轉為誤差已知的三次路徑（詳見擬合、等值線）。
  • 輸出。取樣、JSON、SVG 路徑資料、TikZ，以及 Matplotlib 路徑（詳見取樣與匯出）。

docs.title: 建構與 Hermite 插值
docs.text: 三次曲線由兩個端點及其導數決定。本章的建構方法把這類端點條件轉為控制點，經濟學中只知道幾個數值與斜率的曲線，就是這樣變成 Bézier 曲線。

docs.title: 端點建構
docs.text:
每種建構都是帶有 build() 方法的不可變 dataclass，位於 bezierkit.construction。

EndpointDerivatives(
    start,
    end,
    start_derivative,
    end_derivative
).build()

滿足 \(B(0) =\) start、\(B(1) =\) end、\(B'(0) =\) start_derivative、\(B'(1) =\) end_derivative 的三次曲線，維度不限。

命題 · 端點條件

設 \(P_0, P_3, D_0, D_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d\)。控制點為

\[ P_0, \quad P_0 + D_0 / 3, \quad P_3 - D_1 / 3, \quad P_3 \]

的三次 Bézier 曲線滿足 \(B(0) = P_0\)、\(B(1) = P_3\)、\(B'(0) = D_0\)、\(B'(1) = D_1\)，且它是唯一滿足這些條件、次數不超過 3 的多項式曲線。

TangentDirections(
    start,
    end,
    start_direction,
    end_direction,
    start_handle=1.0,
    end_handle=1.0
).build()

以方向給定端點切線，控制柄長度為 \(|P_1 - P_0| =\) start_handle、\(|P_3 - P_2| =\) end_handle。方向會先正規化，因此只有方向有影響；控制柄長度必須為有限的非負值。依端點條件，\(B'(0)\) 等於 3 倍 start_handle 乘以起點的單位方向。

PlanarSlopes(
    start,
    end,
    start_slope,
    end_slope,
    start_handle=1.0,
    end_handle=1.0
).build()

兩端斜率 \(\mathrm{d} y / \mathrm{d} x\) 為給定值的平面三次曲線，以方向 \((1, m)\) 的 TangentDirections 建構。斜率必須為有限值；垂直切線請改用 TangentDirections。

from bezierkit.construction import PlanarSlopes

demand = PlanarSlopes(
    start=Point(0, 5),
    end=Point(5, 0),
    start_slope=-2,
    end_slope=-0.3,
).build()
# (0.447, 4.106): one unit from (0, 5) along slope -2
print(demand.control_points[1])

docs.title: Hermite 插值
docs.text:
三次 Hermite 插值在區間兩端同時吻合函數值與導數。

定義 · 三次 Hermite 插值多項式

設 \(f\) 在 \([x_0, x_1]\) 上可微，\(x_0 \ne x_1\)。\(f\) 的三次 Hermite 插值多項式是次數不超過 3、滿足

\[ H(x_i) = f(x_i), \quad H'(x_i) = f'(x_i), \quad i = 0, 1 \]

的多項式 \(H\)。對曲線則逐一插值每個座標。

這是 Burden (2011) 第 3.4 節中 Hermite 多項式取兩個節點的情形，該書的定義 3.8。這樣的多項式存在且唯一：

命題 · 存在性與唯一性

三次 Hermite 插值多項式的三次 Hermite 插值多項式存在且唯一。令 \(h = x_1 - x_0\)、\(f_i = f(x_i)\)、\(m_i = f'(x_i)\)，則

\[ H(x) = \sum_{i=0}^3 b_{i,3}((x - x_0) / h) c_i, \]

其中係數為

\[ c_0 = f_0, \quad c_1 = f_0 + h m_0 / 3, \quad c_2 = f_1 - h m_1 / 3, \quad c_3 = f_1. \]

任意節點數的同一結論，見 Stoer (2002) 的定理 (2.1.5.2)。在寬度為 \(h = t_1 - t_0\) 的參數區間 \([t_0, t_1]\) 上，Bézier 線段在 \(s = (t - t_0) / h\) 處求值，導數因此乘上 \(h\)。

parametric_hermite(
    p0,
    p3,
    derivative0,
    derivative1,
    *,
    t0=0.0,
    t1=1.0
)

控制點為 \(P_0\)、\(P_0 + h D_0 / 3\)、\(P_3 - h D_1 / 3\)、\(P_3\) 的三次線段，位於 bezierkit.interpolation。\(h = 0\) 時拋出 ValueError；\(h\) 為負表示反向的區間。

命題 · Hermite 插值

對 parametric_hermite 回傳的線段，令 \(H(t) = B((t - t_0) / h)\)。則 \(H(t_0) = P_0\)、\(H(t_1) = P_3\)、\(H'(t_0) = D_0\)、\(H'(t_1) = D_1\)。

graph_hermite(
    *,
    x0,
    x1,
    y0,
    y1,
    m0,
    m1
)

由函數值 \(y_0 = f(x_0)\)、\(y_1 = f(x_1)\) 與斜率 \(m_0 = f'(x_0)\)、\(m_1 = f'(x_1)\) 得到圖形 \(y = f(x)\) 的插值曲線，即取 \(P = (x, f(x))\)、\(D = (1, f'(x))\)、\(t = x\) 的參數形式。控制點為

\[ (x_0, y_0), \quad (x_0 + h/3, y_0 + h m_0 / 3), \quad (x_1 - h/3, y_1 - h m_1 / 3), \quad (x_1, y_1), \]

其中 \(h = x_1 - x_0\)（參見\(4 / x^2\) 在 \([1, 1.5]\) 的 Hermite 插值。）。

命題 · 圖形形式

graph_hermite 的線段是 \(f\) 在 \([x_0, x_1]\) 上的三次 Hermite 插值多項式 \(H\) 的圖形：即 \(s |\to (x_0 + h s, H(x_0 + h s))\)，\(s \in [0, 1]\)。

from bezierkit.interpolation import graph_hermite

# f(x) = 4 / x^2 on [1, 1.5]
segment = graph_hermite(
    x0=1, x1=1.5, y0=4, y1=16 / 9, m0=-8, m1=-64 / 27
)

docs.title: 插值誤差
docs.text:
定理 · Hermite 誤差界限

設 \(f\) 在 \([x_0, x_1]\) 上四階連續可微，\(x_0 < x_1\)，\(H\) 為其三次 Hermite 插值多項式（詳見三次 Hermite 插值多項式），令 \(h = x_1 - x_0\)、\(M = \max |f^{(4)}|\)。對每個 \(x \in [x_0, x_1]\)，存在 \(\xi \in [x_0, x_1]\) 使

\[ f(x) - H(x) = (f^{(4)}(\xi)) / 24 (x - x_0)^2 (x - x_1)^2, \]

因此

\[ \max_{x \in [x_0, x_1]} |f(x) - H(x)| \le (M h^4) / 384. \]

誤差公式見 Burden (2011) 的定理 3.9（其證明留作該書習題 3.4.11）與 Stoer (2002) 的定理 (2.1.5.9)。此界限是銳利的：對 \([0, 1]\) 上的 \(f(x) = x^4\)，誤差為 \(x^2 (x - 1)^2\)，於 \(x = 1 / 2\) 的最大值 \(1 / 16\) 等於 \(M = 24\) 時的 \(M h^4 / 384\)。

區間減半時界限變為 1/16，自適應擬合正是利用這一點（詳見擬合）。以 \(f(x) = 4 / x^2\) 在 \([1, 1.5]\) 為例，\(f^{(4)}(x) = 480 / x^6\)，故 \(M = 480\)，界限為 \(480 \cdot 0.5^4 / 384 \approx 0.078\)。

hermite_error_bound(
    max_fourth_derivative,
    t0,
    t1
)

Hermite 誤差界限的界限 \(M |t_1 - t_0|^4 / 384\)，位於 bezierkit.fitting。\(M\) 必須為有限的非負值。

此界限適用於純量函數。對曲線 \(t |\to (x(t), y(t))\)，分別套用到每個座標。在 \(\mathbb{R}^d\) 中，歐氏誤差至多為最大座標界限的 \(\sqrt{d}\) 倍，因為對 \(v \in \mathbb{R}^d\) 有 \(\left\lVert v \right\rVert_2 \le \sqrt{d} \left\lVert v \right\rVert_\infty\)（見 Golub (2013) 第 2.2 節）。

docs.title: Bernstein 基底
docs.text:
定義 · Bernstein 多項式

\(n \ge 0\) 次 Bernstein 多項式為

\[ b_{i,n}(t) = \binom{n}{i} t^i (1-t)^{n-i}, \quad i = 0, \ldots, n. \]

其他整數 \(i\) 令 \(b_{i,n} = 0\)。

這組多項式出自 Bernstein (1912)；Farouki (2012)回顧其歷史與性質，三次的情形如三次 Bernstein 多項式。。以下證明用到兩個二項式係數恆等式。

引理 · 二項式恆等式

令 \(n \ge 1\)，\(i\)、\(j\) 為整數，並約定 \(k < 0\) 或 \(k > m\) 時 \(\binom{m}{k} = 0\)。則

\[ \binom{n-1}{j} + \binom{n-1}{j-1} = \binom{n}{j} \]

且

\[ i \binom{n}{i} = n \binom{n-1}{i-1}. \]

命題 · Bernstein 基底

對 \(n \ge 0\)，多項式 \(b_{0,n}, \ldots, b_{n,n}\) 是次數不超過 \(n\) 的實係數多項式向量空間的一組基底。

這是 Floater (2025) 的定理 1.1；證明從頭證明。

命題 · 單位分割

對每個 \(t \in [0, 1]\)，所有 \(b_{i,n}(t) \ge 0\)，且

\[ \sum_{i=0}^n b_{i,n}(t) = 1. \]

定義 · Bézier 曲線

設 \(P_0, \ldots, P_n \in \mathbb{R}^d\)。以 \(P_0, \ldots, P_n\) 為控制點的 \(n\) 次 Bézier 曲線為

\[ B(t) = \sum_{i=0}^n b_{i,n}(t) P_i, \quad t \in [0, 1], \]

其控制多邊形為折線 \(P_0 P_1 \ldots P_n\)。

此定義依循 B{\'e}zier (1966)，形式如 Farin (2002) 與 Prautzsch (2002)。

命題 · 端點

\(b_{i,n}(0)\) 在 \(i = 0\) 時為 1，其餘為 0；\(b_{i,n}(1)\) 在 \(i = n\) 時為 1，其餘為 0。因此 \(B(0) = P_0\)、\(B(1) = P_n\)。

推論 · 凸包

每個 \(B(t)\)（\(t \in [0, 1]\)）都位於控制點 \(P_0, \ldots, P_n\) 的凸包內。

命題 · 仿射不變性

對每個仿射映射 \(A(x) = M x + v\) 與每個 \(t \in [0, 1]\)，

\[ A(B(t)) = \sum_{i=0}^n b_{i,n}(t) A(P_i). \]

變換曲線等同於變換其控制點。

凸包讓曲線不超出控制多邊形所張的區域；仿射不變性則是匯出器與 Matplotlib 轉接器只需移動控制點，就能平移、縮放或旋轉曲線的原因。

BernsteinBasis(int)(float)
BernsteinBasis(int).matrix(values)

某一次數的基底，位於 bezierkit.bezier.basis。在 \(t\) 呼叫時，以陣列回傳 \(i = 0, \ldots, n\) 的 \(b_{i,n}(t)\)；matrix() 對每個參數值回傳一列。

degree

以 PointSet 回傳多個參數下的值。

evaluator

求值策略（見下文）。

不可變的 Bézier 曲線，次數 \(n \ge 0\)、維度 \(d \ge 1\) 均不限，參數範圍為 \([0, 1]\)。points 可為 Point 序列、PointSet、\((n + 1) \times d\) 陣列或 ControlPolygon；所有控制點必須同一維度。

曲線的運算 derivative()、split()、segment() 與 reversed() 詳見導數、反轉與分割。

docs.title: 求值
docs.text:
de Casteljau 演算法以反覆的線性插值計算 \(B(t)\)。

定義 · de Casteljau 點

對參數 \(t\)，令 \(P_i^{(0)} = P_i\)，並對 \(r = 1, \ldots, n\) 令

\[ P_i^{(r)} = (1 - t) P_i^{(r-1)} + t P_{i+1}^{(r-1)}, \quad i = 0, \ldots, n - r. \]

每一輪對相鄰點取平均，多邊形少一個點；\(n\) 輪後只剩一點（參見de Casteljau 演算法 (t = 0.4)。）。此演算法源自 Paul de Casteljau 約 1959 年在 Citroën 的工作 M{\"u}ller (2024)。

定理 · de Casteljau

對 \(0 \le r \le n\) 與 \(0 \le i \le n - r\)，

\[ P_i^{(r)} = \sum_{j=0}^r b_{j,r}(t) P_{i+j}. \]

特別地，\(P_0^{(n)} = B(t)\)。

此敘述見 Floater (2025) 的定理 1.6 與 1.7。

每個中間點都是控制點的凸組合，演算法不會產生互相抵消的大數，因此在高次數時數值穩定。每個參數的計算量為 \(O(n^2)\)。

DeCasteljauEvaluator

預設的求值策略，位於 bezierkit.bezier.evaluation：以 NumPy 一次對整批參數執行上述演算法。

BernsteinEvaluator

以 Bernstein 矩陣乘上控制點。次數低、批次大時較快，但高次數時會加總可能互相抵消的項。依de Casteljau，兩種策略計算的是同一個多項式。

from bezierkit import BezierCurve
from bezierkit.bezier.evaluation import BernsteinEvaluator

fast = BezierCurve(
    curve.control_points, evaluator=BernsteinEvaluator()
)
# Point(coords=(2.0, 1.5)), as with the default
print(fast.at(0.5))

儲存庫的 benchmarks/ 目錄比較兩者在 400、10,000 與 100,000 個參數值下的效能。

docs.title: 升階
docs.text:
\(n\) 次曲線也是 \(n + 1\) 次曲線；新的控制點是舊控制點中相鄰兩點的凸組合。

引理 · 升階恆等式

對 \(n \ge 0\)、\(0 \le i \le n\) 與每個 \(t\)，

\[ b_{i,n}(t) = (n + 1 - i) / (n + 1) b_{i,n+1}(t) + (i + 1) / (n + 1) b_{i+1,n+1}(t). \]

命題 · 升階

設 \(B\) 的控制點為 \(P_0, \ldots, P_n\)。對 \(k = 0, \ldots, n + 1\) 令

\[ Q_k = k / (n + 1) P_{k-1} + (1 - k / (n + 1)) P_k, \]

其中 \(P_{-1}\) 與 \(P_{n+1}\) 可任意選取，因為它們的係數為零。則

\[ B(t) = \sum_{k=0}^{n+1} b_{k,n+1}(t) Q_k \quad \text{對所有} t. \]

曲線及其參數化都不變。

此公式是標準結果 Farin (2002)Prautzsch (2002)；證明的證明不依賴它們。直線與二次曲線的三次表示把它用在直線與二次曲線，也就是本套件需要的情形。

docs.title: 取樣與匯出
docs.text: 匯出器只寫出幾何資料，不選擇顏色、線寬、主題、座標軸、標籤或畫布，也絕不把三次曲線攤平成折線：TikZ 收到原生的 .. controls .. 曲線，SVG 收到原生的 C 指令。

docs.title: 取樣
docs.text:
UniformSampler(int).sample(curve)

在曲線或路徑的定義域上，以 count 個等距參數求值（含兩端，count \(\ge 2\)），位於 bezierkit.sampling。

Sample

取樣的結果：唯讀的參數 t 與 points，提供座標陣列 x、y，並可逐一取出 (t, point)。

from bezierkit.sampling import UniformSampler

sample = UniformSampler(5).sample(curve)
# [0.      0.90625 2.      3.09375 4.     ]
print(sample.x)

docs.title: 四捨五入與座標變換
docs.text:
文字格式的匯出器以固定的小數位數 precision 寫出每個座標，並接受 transform：在寫出前把每個控制點（Point）對應到二維 Point，例如由資料座標轉為頁面座標。

命題 · 四捨五入誤差

設 \(B\)、\(\widetilde{B}\) 是同為 \(n\) 次的 \(\mathbb{R}^d\) 中 Bézier 曲線，控制點分別為 \(P_i\) 與 \(\widetilde{P}_i\)，且對每個 \(i\) 與每個座標 \(k\) 有 \(|\widetilde{P}_{i,k} - P_{i,k}| \le \epsilon\)。則對每個 \(t \in [0, 1]\) 與每個 \(k\)，

\[ |\widetilde{B}_k (t) - B_k (t)| \le \epsilon, \quad \left\lVert \widetilde{B}(t) - B(t) \right\rVert_2 \le \sqrt{d} \epsilon. \]

將每個座標四捨五入到小數點後 \(p\) 位時，\(\epsilon = 1/2 \cdot 10^{-p}\)。

因此在預設的 precision=6 下，匯出的平面曲線處處與原曲線相差不超過 \(0.71 \times 10^{-6}\)，不只在控制點上成立。依仿射不變性，仿射的 transform 是精確的；非仿射的變換能正確移動控制點，但一般不能正確移動控制點之間的曲線。

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
dumps(
    path,
    *,
    metadata=None,
    indent=None
)

位於 bezierkit.export.json。以JSON 路徑格式第 1 版的版本化格式寫出路徑，鍵依字母排序，不含 NaN 或無窮大。

loads(str)

驗證文件並回傳 PathDocument，內含 path 與 metadata。格式或版本不明、線段不是恰好四個點、點的維度不符或數值非有限時，拋出 ValueError。

PathDocument

路徑與呼叫端的 metadata，即 loads() 的回傳值。

schema

字串 "bezierkit.path"

version

整數 1；讀取端拒絕其他版本

dimension

每個點的維度 \(d\)

subpaths

非空陣列，元素為 {"closed": bool, "segments": [...]}，每個線段是四個含 \(d\) 個數值的點

metadata

JSON 物件，原樣傳遞、不解讀

from bezierkit.export.json import dumps, loads

text = dumps(path, metadata={"name": "arch"})
# {"dimension":2,"metadata":{"name":"arch"},"schema":"bezierkit.path",
#  "subpaths":[{"closed":false,"segments":[[[0.0,0.0],[1.0,2.0],...]]}],"version":1}
assert loads(text).path.segments == path.segments

第 1 版已凍結：新增必要的鍵、改變封閉的語意或控制點的排列方式，都需要第 2 版。

from bezierkit.export.svg import to_svg_path_data
